title: Ἄδρηστος
titleEn: Adrastus and the Word of Helenus — Iliad 6.1–115
part: Adrastus and the Word of Helenus (6.1–115)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: With the gods withdrawn, the fighting is left to the men and ranges over the plain between the two rivers. Ajax breaks the Trojan line, and Diomedes, Euryalus and a string of other Achaean captains strike down man after man. Menelaus takes Adrastus alive and is half-persuaded to accept a ransom, until Agamemnon rebukes him and kills the suppliant. Nestor tells the Argives to kill first and strip the dead afterwards. The Trojans are close to being driven back into Ilios when the seer Helenus tells Aeneas and Hector to hold the line while Hector goes to the city to have Athena’s temple opened and a robe and a vow offered against Diomedes. Hector rallies the Trojans, and the Argives give ground, thinking a god has come down to help the enemy.

sentences.t: Τρώων δ’ οἰώθη καὶ Ἀχαιῶν φύλοπις αἰνή·
sentences.tr: Trōōn d’ oiōthē kai Achaiōn phylopis ainē·
sentences.l: Of Trojans and of Achaeans was left alone the fearsome battle-din;
sentences.i: The fearsome din of battle between Trojans and Achaeans was left to itself;
sentences.n: This opens Book 6. οἰώθη is the aorist passive of οἰόομαι ‘be left alone, be left solitary’, and φύλοπις αἰνή is ‘fearsome battle-din’, with the genitives Τρώων and Ἀχαιῶν saying whose it is. At the end of Book 5 Ares was stopped and Hera and Athena went back to Zeus’s house (5.907–909), so the fighting is now left to the men.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθ’ ἴθυσε μάχη πεδίοιο
ἀλλήλων ἰθυνομένων χαλκήρεα δοῦρα
μεσσηγὺς Σιμόεντος ἰδὲ Ξάνθοιο ῥοάων.
sentences.tr:
polla d’ ar’ entha kai enth’ ithyse machē pedioio
allēlōn ithynomenōn chalkērea doura
messēgys Simoentos ide Xanthoio rhoaōn.
sentences.l:
And much, then, here and there rushed the fight over the plain,
of one another aiming the bronze-fitted spears,
between Simois and the streams of Xanthus.
sentences.i: Again and again the fighting rushed here and there over the plain, the men aiming their bronze-fitted spears at one another, between the Simois and the streams of Xanthus.
sentences.n: ἴθυσε is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘rush straight on’, with μάχη as its subject and πεδίοιο the genitive of the ground covered, ‘over the plain’. ἀλλήλων ἰθυνομένων is a genitive absolute, ‘with one another aiming’, and χαλκήρεα δοῦρα ‘bronze-fitted spears’ is what they aim. Σιμόεντος and Ξάνθοιο are the two rivers of the plain, and ῥοάων is the epic genitive plural ‘of the streams’ (= Attic ῥοῶν).

sentences.t:
Αἴας δὲ πρῶτος Τελαμώνιος ἕρκος Ἀχαιῶν
Τρώων ῥῆξε φάλαγγα, φόως δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἔθηκεν,
ἄνδρα βαλὼν ὃς ἄριστος ἐνὶ Θρῄκεσσι τέτυκτο
υἱὸν Ἐϋσσώρου Ἀκάμαντ’ ἠΰν τε μέγαν τε.
sentences.tr:
Aias de prōtos Telamōnios herkos Achaiōn
Trōōn rhēxe phalanga, phoōs d’ hetaroisin ethēken,
andra balōn hos aristos eni Thrēikessi tetykto
huion Eÿssōrou Akamant’ ēÿn te megan te.
sentences.l:
And Ajax first, Telamonian, the fence of the Achaeans,
of the Trojans broke the battle-line, and light to his companions made,
having struck a man who was best among the Thracians,
the son of Eussorus, Acamas, both good and great.
sentences.i: First, Telamonian Ajax, the bulwark of the Achaeans, broke the Trojan line and brought his companions light, by striking the man who was best among the Thracians, Acamas, son of Eussorus, both good and great.
sentences.n: Αἴας … Τελαμώνιος is ‘Telamonian Ajax’, and ἕρκος Ἀχαιῶν ‘bulwark of the Achaeans’ is his stock description, translated every time. πρῶτος says that he is the first to break the Trojan battle-line (φάλαγγα). φόως δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἔθηκεν is literally ‘made light for his companions’: light is the poet’s image for relief, a way out of trouble. βαλών is the aorist participle of βάλλω ‘hit, strike’, and its object ἄνδρα ‘a man’ is named in line 8 as Ἀκάμαντ’ (Ἀκάμαντα) in apposition. Θρῄκεσσι is the epic dative plural in -εσσι. ἠΰν τε μέγαν τε ‘both good and great’ is a pair, and the edition prints the diaeresis in Ἐϋσσώρου.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ἔβαλε πρῶτος κόρυθος φάλον ἱπποδασείης,
ἐν δὲ μετώπῳ πῆξε, πέρησε δ’ ἄρ’ ὀστέον εἴσω
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη· τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν.
sentences.tr:
ton rh’ ebale prōtos korythos phalon hippodaseiēs,
en de metōpōi pēxe, perēse d’ ar’ osteon eisō
aichmē chalkeiē· ton de skotos osse kalypsen.
sentences.l:
him he hit first on the ridge of the horse-haired helmet,
and in the forehead fixed it, and pierced the bone, inside,
the bronze point; and darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: He hit him first on the ridge of his helmet, thick with horsehair, and fixed the spear in his forehead, and the bronze point pierced the bone and went inside; and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: τόν ‘him’ is Acamas, and the subject is still Ajax. ῥ’ is ῥα, the particle ἄρα, and κόρυθος φάλον ἱπποδασείης is ‘the ridge of the helmet, thick with horsehair’, where ἱπποδασείης is the feminine epic genitive in -ης. ἐν … πῆξε is a separated preverb (tmesis): ‘fixed in’. αἰχμὴ χαλκείη ‘the bronze point’ is the subject of πέρησε ‘pierced’ and is held back to line 11. τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν ‘darkness covered his eyes’ is the poem’s regular death formula, with ὄσσε a dual accusative ‘the two eyes’. These three lines are word for word 4.459–461, where another man was struck.

sentences.t:
Ἄξυλον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπεφνε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης
Τευθρανίδην, ὃς ἔναιεν ἐϋκτιμένῃ ἐν Ἀρίσβῃ
ἀφνειὸς βιότοιο, φίλος δ’ ἦν ἀνθρώποισι.
sentences.tr:
Axylon d’ ar’ epephne boēn agathos Diomēdēs
Teuthranidēn, hos enaien eÿktimenēi en Arisbēi
aphneios biotoio, philos d’ ēn anthrōpoisi.
sentences.l:
And Axylus then slew, good at the war-cry, Diomedes,
Teuthras’-son, who lived in well-built Arisbe,
rich in livelihood, and was dear to men.
sentences.i: Diomedes, good at the war-cry, killed Axylus, son of Teuthras, who lived in well-built Arisbe, rich in livelihood, and was dear to men.
sentences.n: The object comes first: Ἄξυλον is the man killed, and Διομήδης (with the stock epithet βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’) is the killer. ἔπεφνε is an old aorist ‘slew’, and Τευθρανίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Teuthras’. ἐϋκτιμένῃ ‘well-built’ keeps the edition’s diaeresis, and ἀφνειὸς βιότοιο ‘rich in livelihood’ has the epic genitive -οιο. Ἀρίσβῃ is a town; nothing more is said of it here.

sentences.t: πάντας γὰρ φιλέεσκεν ὁδῷ ἔπι οἰκία ναίων.
sentences.tr: pantas gar phileesken hodōi epi oikia naiōn.
sentences.l: for all he used to love, dwelling in a house by the road.
sentences.i: for he used to love them all, living in his house beside the road.
sentences.n: φιλέεσκεν is an iterative imperfect in -εσκον, ‘used to love’: this was his habit. ὁδῷ ἔπι is ἐπὶ ὁδῷ with the preposition placed after its noun, ‘beside the road’. οἰκία ναίων ‘dwelling in a house’ uses the plural οἰκία for one dwelling. The line gives the reason for φίλος ἀνθρώποισι in the line before: his house stood on the road, and his friendliness to those who passed was what made him dear to men.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά οἱ οὔ τις τῶν γε τότ’ ἤρκεσε λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον
πρόσθεν ὑπαντιάσας, ἀλλ’ ἄμφω θυμὸν ἀπηύρα
αὐτὸν καὶ θεράποντα Καλήσιον, ὅς ῥα τόθ’ ἵππων
ἔσκεν ὑφηνίοχος·
sentences.tr:
alla hoi ou tis tōn ge tot’ ērkese lygron olethron
prosthen hypantiasas, all’ amphō thymon apēura
auton kai theraponta Kalēsion, hos rha toth’ hippōn
esken hyphēniochos·
sentences.l:
but for him none of those men then warded off grievous destruction,
in front, having gone to meet it; but both of them the life he took from,
himself and his attendant Calesius, who then of the horses
was the charioteer;
sentences.i: But none of those men then warded off grievous destruction from him by going out in front to meet the attack; Diomedes took the life from both of them, Axylus himself and his attendant Calesius, who was then the driver of his horses;
sentences.n: οἱ ‘for him’ is Axylus, and τῶν γε τότ’ ‘of those then’ with οὔ τις gives ‘none of those men’. ἤρκεσε … λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον is ‘warded off grievous destruction’, as at 2.873; πρόσθεν ὑπαντιάσας ‘having gone to meet it in front’ is the way a man shields another. ἀπηύρα is the aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take away from’, with a double accusative: ἄμφω ‘both’ (the men) and θυμόν ‘life’ (the thing taken). αὐτὸν καὶ θεράποντα Καλήσιον explains ἄμφω. ἔσκεν is an old imperfect of εἰμί in -σκ-, ‘was’, and ὑφηνίοχος is ‘charioteer’. English needs a subject for ἀπηύρα, and the unit supplies Diomedes from line 12.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ ἄμφω γαῖαν ἐδύτην.
sentences.tr: tō d’ amphō gaian edytēn.
sentences.l: and the two both the earth entered.
sentences.i: and the two of them entered the earth.
sentences.n: ἐδύτην is a dual (aorist of δύω ‘go into, sink into’), agreeing with τὼ … ἄμφω ‘the two, both’. To enter the earth (γαῖαν ἐδύτην, an accusative of place with no preposition) is the poet’s way of saying that they died.

sentences.t: Δρῆσον δ’ Εὐρύαλος καὶ Ὀφέλτιον ἐξενάριξε·
sentences.tr: Drēson d’ Euryalos kai Opheltion exenarixe·
sentences.l: And Dresus and Opheltius Euryalus despoiled;
sentences.i: Euryalus killed Dresus and Opheltius and stripped them of their armour;
sentences.n: Again the objects stand first (Δρῆσον … Ὀφέλτιον) and the subject Εὐρύαλος after them. ἐξενάριξε comes from ἐναρίζω, ‘strip the ἔναρα (the armour of a slain man)’, and so it names both the killing and the stripping in one word, as the English says.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ μετ’ Αἴσηπον καὶ Πήδασον, οὕς ποτε νύμφη
νηῒς Ἀβαρβαρέη τέκ’ ἀμύμονι Βουκολίωνι.
sentences.tr:
bē de met’ Aisēpon kai Pēdason, hous pote nymphē
nēïs Abarbareē tek’ amymoni Boukoliōni.
sentences.l:
and he went after Aesepus and Pedasus, whom once a nymph,
a naiad, Abarbarea, bore to blameless Bucolion.
sentences.i: He went after Aesepus and Pedasus, whom the naiad nymph Abarbarea once bore to blameless Bucolion.
sentences.n: βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω without the augment, and βῆ δὲ μετά + accusative is ‘went after’, the verb of attack; Euryalus is still the subject. οὕς is the relative ‘whom’, and τέκ’ is τέκε, the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω ‘bear’. νηῒς is ‘naiad’, a water-nymph. ἀμύμονι ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet, translated every time, even of a man whose birth the next lines call secret.

sentences.t:
Βουκολίων δ’ ἦν υἱὸς ἀγαυοῦ Λαομέδοντος
πρεσβύτατος γενεῇ, σκότιον δέ ἑ γείνατο μήτηρ·
sentences.tr:
Boukoliōn d’ ēn huios agauou Laomedontos
presbytatos geneēi, skotion de he geinato mētēr·
sentences.l:
And Bucolion was son of noble Laomedon,
eldest by birth, but in secret his mother bore him;
sentences.i: Bucolion was the eldest son of noble Laomedon, though his mother had borne him in secret;
sentences.n: ἀγαυοῦ ‘noble’ is a stock epithet, here of Laomedon, and πρεσβύτατος γενεῇ is ‘eldest by birth’ (dative of respect). σκότιον is literally ‘in the dark’ (neuter, used as an adverb), and it means that the child was born out of wedlock. ἑ is the epic accusative pronoun ‘him’ (= αὐτόν).

sentences.t:
ποιμαίνων δ’ ἐπ’ ὄεσσι μίγη φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ,
ἣ δ’ ὑποκυσαμένη διδυμάονε γείνατο παῖδε.
sentences.tr:
poimainōn d’ ep’ oessi migē philotēti kai eunēi,
hē d’ hypokysamenē didymaone geinato paide.
sentences.l:
and tending sheep, he mingled in love and in bed,
and she, having conceived, bore twin sons.
sentences.i: While he was tending his sheep he joined with her in love and in bed, and she conceived and bore twin sons.
sentences.n: ποιμαίνων ‘shepherding’ goes with ἐπ’ ὄεσσι ‘over his sheep’ (ὄεσσι is the epic dative plural of ὄϊς). μίγη is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι, ‘was joined’, and the nymph is understood as the one he joined; φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ ‘in love and in bed’ are two datives. ἣ δ’ is ‘and she’, the nymph. ὑποκυσαμένη is the aorist participle of ὑποκύω ‘conceive’, and διδυμάονε παῖδε is a dual, ‘twin sons’.

sentences.t:
καὶ μὲν τῶν ὑπέλυσε μένος καὶ φαίδιμα γυῖα
Μηκιστηϊάδης καὶ ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἐσύλα.
sentences.tr:
kai men tōn hypelyse menos kai phaidima guia
Mēkistēïadēs kai ap’ ōmōn teuche’ esyla.
sentences.l:
And indeed of these loosened the might and the glorious limbs
the Mecisteus’-son, and from their shoulders the armour was stripping.
sentences.i: Then the son of Mecisteus loosened the might and the glorious limbs of these two, and stripped the armour from their shoulders.
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of these’ are the twin sons. ὑπέλυσε μένος καὶ φαίδιμα γυῖα ‘loosened the might and the glorious limbs’ is how the poet says a man was killed: the limbs lose their strength. Μηκιστηϊάδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Mecisteus’, and is Euryalus, who has been the subject since line 20. ἐσύλα is an imperfect, ‘was stripping’, from συλάω. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is a stock epithet; καὶ μέν is ‘and indeed’.

sentences.t: Ἀστύαλον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπεφνε μενεπτόλεμος Πολυποίτης·
sentences.tr: Astyalon d’ ar’ epephne meneptolemos Polypoitēs·
sentences.l: And Astyalus then slew, steadfast-in-battle Polypoetes;
sentences.i: Polypoetes, steadfast in battle, killed Astyalus;
sentences.n: The word order is object first again: Ἀστύαλον is the victim and μενεπτόλεμος Πολυποίτης the killer. μενεπτόλεμος ‘steadfast in battle’ is the stock epithet, one who stays in the fight.

sentences.t:
Πιδύτην δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς Περκώσιον ἐξενάριξεν
ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ, Τεῦκρος δ’ Ἀρετάονα δῖον.
sentences.tr:
Pidytēn d’ Odyseus Perkōsion exenarixen
encheï chalkeiōi, Teukros d’ Aretaona dion.
sentences.l:
And Pidytes the Percosian Odysseus despoiled
with a bronze spear, and Teucer heavenly Aretaon.
sentences.i: Odysseus killed Pidytes of Percote with a bronze spear and stripped him of his armour, and Teucer did the same to heavenly Aretaon.
sentences.n: Περκώσιον is the adjective from the town of Percote (‘of Percote’). ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ is a dative of instrument, ‘with a bronze spear’. Τεῦκρος δ’ has no verb of its own: ἐξενάριξεν from the first half is understood for him, and the English supplies ‘did the same’. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δ’ Ἄβληρον ἐνήρατο δουρὶ φαεινῷ
Νεστορίδης, Ἔλατον δὲ ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr:
Antilochos d’ Ablēron enērato douri phaeinōi
Nestoridēs, Elaton de anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l:
And Antilochus Ablerus slew with a shining spear,
the son of Nestor, and Elatus the lord of men, Agamemnon;
sentences.i: Antilochus, son of Nestor, killed Ablerus with his shining spear, and Agamemnon, lord of men, killed Elatus;
sentences.n: ἐνήρατο is the aorist middle of ἐναίρω ‘kill’. Νεστορίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Nestor’, in apposition to Ἀντίλοχος, and δουρί is the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’ (the old stem δουρ-). Ἔλατον has no verb: ἐνήρατο is carried over, and the English says ‘killed’ again. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock title.

sentences.t:
ναῖε δὲ Σατνιόεντος ἐϋρρείταο παρ’ ὄχθας
Πήδασον αἰπεινήν.
sentences.tr:
naie de Satnioentos eÿrreitao par’ ochthas
Pēdason aipeinēn.
sentences.l:
and he dwelt by the banks of fair-flowing Satnioeis
in steep Pedasus.
sentences.i: He lived by the banks of the fair-flowing Satnioeis, in steep Pedasus.
sentences.n: ναῖε is an imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’ with a plain accusative of place, Πήδασον αἰπεινήν ‘steep Pedasus’. The verb has no named subject, and the man last named is Elatus (line 33). Σατνιόεντος ἐϋρρείταο has the epic genitive in -αο (= Attic -ου), and ἐϋρρείταο ‘fair-flowing’ keeps the diaeresis. Pedasus is also the name of one of Bucolion’s sons (line 21).

sentences.t:
Φύλακον δ’ ἕλε Λήϊτος ἥρως
φεύγοντ’·
sentences.tr:
Phylakon d’ hele Lēïtos hērōs
pheugont’·
sentences.l:
And Phylacus took, Leitus the hero,
fleeing;
sentences.i: The hero Leitus killed Phylacus as he fled;
sentences.n: Object first again: Φύλακον is the man caught and Λήϊτος ἥρως ‘Leitus the hero’ the subject. ἕλε is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take, catch’; in a list of killings it means that he killed him, and where the poet means a capture he has to say so (ζωὸν ἕλ’ ‘took alive’ at line 38). φεύγοντ’ is the elided accusative participle φεύγοντα ‘fleeing’, agreeing with Φύλακον.

sentences.t: Εὐρύπυλος δὲ Μελάνθιον ἐξενάριξεν.
sentences.tr: Eurypylos de Melanthion exenarixen.
sentences.l: and Melanthius Eurypylus despoiled.
sentences.i: Eurypylus killed Melanthius and stripped him of his armour.
sentences.n: This ends the run of quick killings on the verb that has carried it (ἐξενάριξεν, as at lines 20 and 30). The object Μελάνθιον stands before the subject Εὐρύπυλος. The scene of Adrastus, which takes more room, follows.

sentences.t:
Ἄδρηστον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
ζωὸν ἕλ’·
sentences.tr:
Adrēston d’ ar’ epeita boēn agathos Menelaos
zōon hel’·
sentences.l:
And Adrastus then next, Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
took alive;
sentences.i: Next Menelaus, good at the war-cry, took Adrastus alive;
sentences.n: Ἄδρηστον is the object and βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος the subject, with the stock epithet ‘good at the war-cry’. ζωὸν ἕλ’ (ἕλε) is ‘took alive’, a capture, in contrast to ἕλε at line 35. The rest of the sentence says how it came about: an accident to Adrastus’s chariot.

sentences.t:
ἵππω γάρ οἱ ἀτυζομένω πεδίοιο
ὄζῳ ἔνι βλαφθέντε μυρικίνῳ ἀγκύλον ἅρμα
ἄξαντ’ ἐν πρώτῳ ῥυμῷ αὐτὼ μὲν ἐβήτην
πρὸς πόλιν, ᾗ περ οἱ ἄλλοι ἀτυζόμενοι φοβέοντο,
sentences.tr:
hippō gar hoi atyzomenō pedioio
ozōi eni blaphthente myrikinōi ankylon harma
axant’ en prōtōi rhymōi autō men ebētēn
pros polin, hēi per hoi alloi atyzomenoi phobeonto,
sentences.l:
for his two horses, dazed with fear over the plain,
in a tamarisk branch hindered, the curved chariot
having broken at the end of the pole, themselves went off
to the city, just where the others, dazed with fear, were fleeing,
sentences.i: For his two horses, dazed with fear on the plain, were caught in a tamarisk branch and broke the curved chariot at the end of the pole, and they themselves went off toward the city, just where the rest were fleeing, dazed with fear,
sentences.n: ἵππω, ἀτυζομένω, βλαφθέντε, ἄξαντ’ and αὐτώ are all duals (the pair of horses), and their one verb, ἐβήτην (dual aorist of βαίνω), waits until line 40: the sentence is held up by participles. ἀτυζομένω is ‘dazed with fear’ (ἀτύζομαι), and the plural ἀτυζόμενοι at the end of the unit says the same of the others. ὄζῳ ἔνι … μυρικίνῳ is ἐν ὄζῳ μυρικίνῳ ‘in a tamarisk branch’, with ἔνι after its noun. βλαφθέντε is the aorist passive participle of βλάπτω ‘hinder, damage’. ἐν πρώτῳ ῥυμῷ is ‘at the end of the pole’ (the ῥυμός is the chariot pole), and ἀγκύλον ‘curved’ describes ἅρμα. ᾗ περ is ‘just where’, and φοβέοντο is the imperfect middle of φοβέομαι ‘be put to flight’. οἱ in line 38 is ‘his’ (Adrastus’s).

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐκ δίφροιο παρὰ τροχὸν ἐξεκυλίσθη
πρηνὴς ἐν κονίῃσιν ἐπὶ στόμα·
sentences.tr:
autos d’ ek diphroio para trochon exekylisthē
prēnēs en koniēisin epi stoma·
sentences.l:
and he himself from the chariot beside the wheel was rolled out,
headlong in the dust, on his mouth;
sentences.i: and he himself was rolled out of the chariot beside the wheel, headlong in the dust, down on his mouth;
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Adrastus, set against his horses, which have gone. ἐξεκυλίσθη is the aorist passive of ἐκκυλίω ‘roll out’, and παρὰ τροχόν ‘beside the wheel’ says where he came down. πρηνής is ‘headlong, face down’, κονίῃσιν is the epic dative plural ‘in the dust’, and ἐπὶ στόμα ‘on his mouth’ is the usual way of saying that a man lay on his face.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δέ οἱ ἔστη
Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος ἔχων δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
par de hoi estē
Atreïdēs Menelaos echōn dolichoskion enchos.
sentences.l:
and beside him stood
Atreus’-son Menelaus, holding his long-shadowed spear.
sentences.i: and Menelaus, son of Atreus, stood beside him, holding his long-shadowed spear.
sentences.n: πὰρ … ἔστη is a verb split by tmesis, ‘stood beside’, with οἱ ‘by him’ between the halves. Both brothers are Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’, and the name Μενέλαος added here shows that it is Menelaus; at line 64 the same word means Agamemnon. δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος is ‘long-shadowed spear’, from δολιχός ‘long’ and σκιά ‘shadow’.

sentences.t: Ἄδρηστος δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα λαβὼν ἐλίσσετο γούνων·
sentences.tr: Adrēstos d’ ar’ epeita labōn elisseto gounōn·
sentences.l: And Adrastus then next, having taken hold of his knees, entreated him;
sentences.i: Then Adrastus took hold of his knees and begged him:
sentences.n: ἄρ’ ἔπειτα ‘and then’ takes up the story again. λαβὼν γούνων ‘taking hold of his knees’ is the suppliant’s grip (as Thetis does at 1.500), and ἐλίσσετο is the imperfect of λίσσομαι ‘beg, entreat’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: in the fourth foot the ἐ- of ἐλίσσετο has to count long, as if the word were spelled ἐλλίσσετο.

sentences.t: ζώγρει Ἀτρέος υἱέ, σὺ δ’ ἄξια δέξαι ἄποινα·
sentences.tr: zōgrei Atreos huie, sy d’ axia dexai apoina·
sentences.l: “Take me alive, son of Atreus, and you accept worthy ransom;
sentences.i: “Take me alive, son of Atreus, and accept a ransom of full worth;
sentences.n: ζώγρει is the imperative of ζωγρέω ‘take alive’, the plea of a man who asks to be a prisoner and not a corpse. Ἀτρέος υἱέ is the vocative ‘son of Atreus’, with the genitive Ἀτρέος of Ἀτρεύς. ἄξια ‘of worth’ agrees with ἄποινα ‘ransom’, the price paid for a captive. δέξαι is the aorist imperative middle of δέχομαι ‘accept’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δ’ ἐν ἀφνειοῦ πατρὸς κειμήλια κεῖται
χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε σίδηρος,
τῶν κέν τοι χαρίσαιτο πατὴρ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα
εἴ κεν ἐμὲ ζωὸν πεπύθοιτ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
polla d’ en aphneiou patros keimēlia keitai
chalkos te chrysos te polykmētos te sidēros,
tōn ken toi charisaito patēr apereisi’ apoina
ei ken eme zōon pepythoit’ epi nēusin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
Many treasures lie in a wealthy father’s house,
bronze and gold and much-laboured iron,
of these my father would grant you unstinted ransom,
if me alive he should learn of at the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: In my wealthy father’s house many treasures lie: bronze and gold and iron worked with much labour. From these my father would grant you an unstinted ransom, if he were to learn that I am alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: Adrastus names what he can pay. κειμήλια are ‘treasures’, wealth laid up in the house (ἐν ἀφνειοῦ πατρός leaves out ‘house’), and the line χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε σίδηρος ‘bronze and gold and much-laboured iron’ is a line the Odyssey also uses: πολύκμητος is ‘worked with much toil’, and iron is listed with the precious metals. τῶν κέν τοι χαρίσαιτο ‘of these he would grant you’ has κεν with the optative for ‘would’, and τοι is ‘to you’ (= σοι). ἀπερείσι’ is ἀπερείσια ‘unstinted’, elided. εἴ κεν … πεπύθοιτ’ is ‘if he should learn’ (an optative of πυνθάνομαι with a reduplicated stem), and ἐμὲ ζωόν is ‘me alive’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔπειθε·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tōi d’ ara thymon eni stēthessin epeithe·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in him the heart in his breast he was persuading;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he was winning over the heart in Menelaus’ breast;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ is the speech-closing formula, with φάτο unaugmented. The second half is made like 4.208, where the heart is stirred (ὄρινε) in Machaon’s breast; here the verb is ἔπειθε ‘was persuading’, an imperfect, because the persuasion is under way when Agamemnon breaks in. τῷ ‘in him’ names whose heart, Menelaus’s, and θυμόν is the object. ἐνί is ἐν ‘in’, and στήθεσσιν is the epic dative plural.

sentences.t:
καὶ δή μιν τάχ’ ἔμελλε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
δώσειν ᾧ θεράποντι καταξέμεν·
sentences.tr:
kai dē min tach’ emelle thoas epi nēas Achaiōn
dōsein hōi theraponti kataxemen·
sentences.l:
And indeed him soon he was about, to the swift ships of the Achaeans,
to give to his own attendant to lead down;
sentences.i: And Menelaus was on the point of handing him over to his own attendant, to be led down to the swift ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: καὶ δή … τάχ’ ἔμελλε ‘and now he was soon to …’ sets up the interruption, and ἔμελλε with the future infinitive δώσειν is ‘was about to give’. μιν is ‘him’, Adrastus. ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’ (ὅς, ἥ, ὅν), not the relative; the attendant (θεράποντι) would take him down to the ships (θοάς ‘swift’, the stock epithet). καταξέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (= Attic -ειν) of κατάγω ‘lead down’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
ἀντίος ἦλθε θέων, καὶ ὁμοκλήσας ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
all’ Agamemnōn
antios ēlthe theōn, kai homoklēsas epos ēuda·
sentences.l:
but Agamemnon
opposite came running, and having shouted at him spoke a word:
sentences.i: but Agamemnon came running to meet him and, shouting at him, said:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ‘but’ marks the interruption. ἀντίος is ‘opposite, face to face’ (used as an adverb), and ἦλθε θέων is ‘came running’ (θέων, participle of θέω). ὁμοκλήσας is the aorist participle of ὁμοκλέω ‘shout at, rebuke’ (the same verb as at 5.439); ἔπος ηὔδα is ‘spoke a word’, with ηὔδα an imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπον ὦ Μενέλαε, τί ἢ δὲ σὺ κήδεαι οὕτως
ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.tr:
ō pepon ō Menelae, ti ē de sy kēdeai houtōs
andrōn;
sentences.l:
“O good one, O Menelaus, why then do you care so
for men?
sentences.i: “My good fellow, Menelaus, why do you care so much for these men?
sentences.n: ὦ πέπον ‘O good one’ is a familiar address, and the exact sense of πέπον is not known. τί ἢ δὲ … ‘why, then …’ sharpens the question into a reproach. κήδεαι is the second person singular of κήδομαι ‘care for’, taking the genitive ἀνδρῶν; the word ‘men’ is just that, and the next lines show that they are the Trojans. Agamemnon’s speech runs to line 60.

sentences.t:
ἦ σοὶ ἄριστα πεποίηται κατὰ οἶκον
πρὸς Τρώων;
sentences.tr:
ē soi arista pepoiētai kata oikon
pros Trōōn;
sentences.l:
Truly for you the best has been done in your house
by the Trojans?
sentences.i: Can it be that the Trojans have treated you so very well at home?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a yes-or-no question, here a bitter one. πεποίηται is the perfect passive of ποιέω, and ἄριστα ‘the best things’ is its subject, so the Greek is literally ‘has the best been done for you …?’, with the agent given by πρὸς Τρώων ‘by the Trojans’. κατὰ οἶκον is ‘at home, in your house’. The question is sarcasm: Agamemnon means that the Trojans have done Menelaus no good at all.

sentences.t:
τῶν μή τις ὑπεκφύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον
χεῖράς θ’ ἡμετέρας, μηδ’ ὅν τινα γαστέρι μήτηρ
κοῦρον ἐόντα φέροι, μηδ’ ὃς φύγοι, ἀλλ’ ἅμα πάντες
Ἰλίου ἐξαπολοίατ’ ἀκήδεστοι καὶ ἄφαντοι.
sentences.tr:
tōn mē tis hypekphygoi aipyn olethron
cheiras th’ hēmeteras, mēd’ hon tina gasteri mētēr
kouron eonta pheroi, mēd’ hos phygoi, all’ hama pantes
Iliou exapoloiat’ akēdestoi kai aphantoi.
sentences.l:
of them let no one escape steep destruction
and our hands, nor whomever his mother in her belly
bears, being a boy, nor who might escape, but altogether all
from Ilios perish, unmourned and unseen.”
sentences.i: Let none of them escape steep destruction and our hands, not even the boy a mother carries in her belly, nor anyone who might flee, but let them all perish together out of Ilios, unmourned and unseen.”
sentences.n: The whole sentence is a wish in the optative: μή τις ὑπεκφύγοι ‘let no one escape’, with αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον ‘steep destruction’ and χεῖράς θ’ ἡμετέρας ‘and our hands’ as its two objects. τῶν ‘of them’ means the Trojans. μηδ’ ὅν τινα … φέροι ‘nor any whom a mother carries’, with κοῦρον ἐόντα ‘being a boy’, is a male child still in the womb; μηδ’ ὃς φύγοι is ‘nor anyone who might flee’. ἐξαπολοίατ’ is the aorist optative middle of ἐξαπόλλυμι ‘perish utterly’, and Ἰλίου is a genitive of separation, ‘out of Ilios’. ἀκήδεστοι ‘unmourned’ comes from the same root as κήδεαι ‘you care’ in line 55, and ἄφαντοι is ‘unseen’, gone without trace. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἔτρεψεν ἀδελφειοῦ φρένας ἥρως
αἴσιμα παρειπών·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn etrepsen adelpheiou phrenas hērōs
aisima pareipōn·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he turned his brother’s mind, the hero,
fitting things having talked-over;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the hero turned his brother’s mind, talking him round with what was fitting;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes the speech, and ἥρως ‘the hero’ is Agamemnon. ἀδελφειοῦ is the genitive of ἀδελφειός, an epic form of ἀδελφός ‘brother’, and φρένας is the plural of φρήν, the seat of thought, ‘mind’. παρειπών is the aorist participle of παρεῖπον ‘talk over, persuade’, with αἴσιμα ‘fitting things’ (neuter plural) as what he said.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀπὸ ἕθεν ὤσατο χειρὶ
ἥρω’ Ἄδρηστον·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ apo hethen ōsato cheiri
hērō’ Adrēston·
sentences.l:
and he from himself pushed with his hand
the hero Adrastus;
sentences.i: and Menelaus pushed the hero Adrastus away from himself with his hand;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Menelaus (the article-form as a pronoun). ἕθεν is the epic genitive of the reflexive pronoun, ‘from himself’, after ἀπό, and ὤσατο is the aorist middle of ὠθέω ‘push’. χειρί is a dative of instrument. ἥρω’ is the elided accusative ἥρωα: Adrastus gets the title ‘hero’ like any warrior.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
οὖτα κατὰ λαπάρην·
sentences.tr:
ton de kreiōn Agamemnōn
outa kata laparēn·
sentences.l:
and him lord Agamemnon
wounded in the flank;
sentences.i: and lord Agamemnon stabbed him in the flank;
sentences.n: τὸν δέ ‘and him’ is Adrastus. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘lord Agamemnon’, with the house rendering ‘lord’ for κρείων. οὖτα is an aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound with a thrust’, and κατὰ λαπάρην is ‘in the flank’, the soft part of the side below the ribs.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀνετράπετ’, Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ
λὰξ ἐν στήθεσι βὰς ἐξέσπασε μείλινον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ anetrapet’, Atreïdēs de
lax en stēthesi bas exespase meilinon enchos.
sentences.l:
and he was overturned, and Atreus’-son
with his heel on his chest, having stepped, drew out the ashen spear.
sentences.i: and he fell over, and the son of Atreus, setting his heel on his chest, pulled out the ashen spear.
sentences.n: ἀνετράπετ’ is the aorist middle of ἀνατρέπω ‘turn over’: the stabbed man is knocked down. Here Ἀτρεΐδης is Agamemnon, who did the stabbing, and not Menelaus (compare line 44). λάξ ‘with the heel’ goes with βάς, the aorist participle of βαίνω ‘having stepped’, and ἐξέσπασε is the aorist of ἐκσπάω ‘pull out’. μείλινον ‘ashen’ is the spear’s stock epithet, from μελίη ‘ash-tree’.

sentences.t: Νέστωρ δ’ Ἀργείοισιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr: Nestōr d’ Argeioisin ekekleto makron aÿsas·
sentences.l: And Nestor to the Argives called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Nestor gave orders to the Argives, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: ἐκέκλετο is the aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘call upon, give orders to’, and ἀΰσας is the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’; μακρόν, literally ‘long’, is used as an adverb for ‘loudly’ (as at 5.347). The line is a formula, and it returns at line 110 with Hector and the Trojans. Ἀργείοισιν is the epic dative plural, and ‘Argives’ is one of the three names for the army, kept in both layers.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἥρωες Δαναοὶ θεράποντες Ἄρηος
μή τις νῦν ἐνάρων ἐπιβαλλόμενος μετόπισθε
μιμνέτω ὥς κε πλεῖστα φέρων ἐπὶ νῆας ἵκηται,
ἀλλ’ ἄνδρας κτείνωμεν·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi hērōes Danaoi therapontes Arēos
mē tis nyn enarōn epiballomenos metopisthe
mimnetō hōs ke pleista pherōn epi nēas hikētai,
all’ andras kteinōmen·
sentences.l:
“O friends, heroes, Danaans, attendants of Ares,
let no one now, falling upon the spoils, behind
stay, so that carrying the most he may come to the ships,
but let us kill men;
sentences.i: “Friends, Danaan heroes, attendants of Ares: let no one now stay behind, throwing himself on the spoils so as to reach the ships carrying the most; no, let us kill men,
sentences.n: The address is the line Agamemnon used at 2.110, and the English is the same: θεράποντες Ἄρηος ‘attendants of Ares’ makes the warriors the war-god’s servants (Ἄρηος is the epic genitive). μή τις … μιμνέτω is ‘let no one stay’, a third-person imperative with μή. ἐπιβαλλόμενος is ‘throwing himself upon’, ἐνάρων is ‘spoils’ (the ἔναρα, armour stripped from the dead, as in ἐξενάριξε), and μετόπισθε is ‘behind’. ὥς κε … ἵκηται is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come, reach’. κτείνωμεν is the subjunctive used as ‘let us kill’.

sentences.t:
ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ τὰ ἕκηλοι
νεκροὺς ἂμ πεδίον συλήσετε τεθνηῶτας.
sentences.tr:
epeita de kai ta hekēloi
nekrous am pedion sylēsete tethnēōtas.
sentences.l:
and afterwards, that too, at ease,
the corpses along the plain you will strip, the dead.”
sentences.i: Afterwards you can strip the dead across the plain at your ease.”
sentences.n: συλήσετε is a future used as a permission, ‘you shall (be able to) strip’. ἕκηλοι ‘at ease’ agrees with ‘you’, and καὶ τά ‘that too’ points to the stripping as the later business. ἂμ πεδίον is ἀνὰ πεδίον ‘along, over the plain’ (ἀνά before π is written ἂμ). νεκροὺς … τεθνηῶτας is ‘the corpses, the dead’, a doubling that stresses death, and τεθνηῶτας is the epic perfect participle of θνῄσκω (Attic τεθνεῶτας). The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes the speech. ὄτρυνε is the unaugmented aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, with μένος καὶ θυμόν ‘the might and the heart’ as object and ἑκάστου ‘of each man’. The line is word for word 5.470.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κεν αὖτε Τρῶες ἀρηϊφίλων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν
Ἴλιον εἰσανέβησαν ἀναλκείῃσι δαμέντες,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ Αἰνείᾳ τε καὶ Ἕκτορι εἶπε παραστὰς
Πριαμίδης Ἕλενος οἰωνοπόλων ὄχ’ ἄριστος·
sentences.tr:
entha ken aute Trōes arēïphilōn hyp’ Achaiōn
Ilion eisanebēsan analkeiēisi damentes,
ei mē ar’ Aineiāi te kai Hektori eipe parastas
Priamidēs Helenos oiōnopolōn och’ aristos·
sentences.l:
There, again, the Trojans, by the Ares-loved Achaeans
to Ilios would have gone up, overcome through want of might,
if not then to Aeneas and to Hector had spoken, standing beside them,
Priam’s-son Helenus, of bird-diviners by far the best:
sentences.i: Then once more the Trojans, overcome by the Achaeans, dear to Ares, through their want of might, would have gone up into Ilios, had not Helenus, son of Priam, far the best of those who read the birds, stood beside Aeneas and Hector and spoken to them:
sentences.n: ἔνθά κεν … εἰσανέβησαν is κεν with the aorist indicative, ‘would have gone up’, a thing that did not happen; εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ … εἶπε ‘if … had not spoken’ gives the condition. εἰσανέβησαν is the aorist of εἰσαναβαίνω ‘go up into’, and ‘up’ because Ilios stands on a height. ἀρηϊφίλων ‘dear to Ares’ is a stock epithet, here of the Achaeans. δαμέντες is the aorist passive participle of δαμάζω ‘overcome’, and ἀναλκείῃσι is the dative plural of ἀναλκείη ‘want of ἀλκή’ (the ἀλκή of line 112, ‘might’). Πριαμίδης Ἕλενος is ‘Helenus, son of Priam’, and οἰωνοπόλων ὄχ’ ἄριστος is the phrase used of Calchas at 1.69, ‘far the best of those who read the birds’. παραστάς is ‘standing beside’.

sentences.t:
Αἰνεία τε καὶ Ἕκτορ, ἐπεὶ πόνος ὔμμι μάλιστα
Τρώων καὶ Λυκίων ἐγκέκλιται, οὕνεκ’ ἄριστοι
πᾶσαν ἐπ’ ἰθύν ἐστε μάχεσθαί τε φρονέειν τε,
στῆτ’ αὐτοῦ,
sentences.tr:
Aineia te kai Hektor, epei ponos ymmi malista
Trōōn kai Lykiōn enkeklitai, hounek’ aristoi
pasan ep’ ithyn este machesthai te phroneein te,
stēt’ autou,
sentences.l:
“Aeneas and Hector, since the toil on you most
of Trojans and Lycians has leaned, because you are best
on every straight course, both to fight and to think,
stand here,
sentences.i: “Aeneas and Hector, since the labour rests most heavily on you, of all the Trojans and Lycians, because you are the best at every turn, both at fighting and at thinking, stand your ground here,
sentences.n: Αἰνεία and Ἕκτορ are vocatives. ὔμμι is the Aeolic form of ὑμῖν ‘to you’. πόνος … ἐγκέκλιται is ‘the toil has leaned (on you)’, the perfect passive of ἐγκλίνω ‘lean on’, and Τρώων καὶ Λυκίων is a partitive genitive with μάλιστα: ‘most of all the Trojans and Lycians’. οὕνεκ’ is ‘because’. πᾶσαν ἐπ’ ἰθύν is literally ‘on every straight course’, that is, whichever way things go. μάχεσθαί τε φρονέειν τε are two infinitives ‘to fight and to think’ (φρονέειν = φρονεῖν) after ἄριστοι. στῆτ’ is the aorist imperative of ἵστημι ‘stand’, and αὐτοῦ is ‘right here’. Helenus’s speech runs to line 101.

sentences.t:
καὶ λαὸν ἐρυκάκετε πρὸ πυλάων
πάντῃ ἐποιχόμενοι πρὶν αὖτ’ ἐν χερσὶ γυναικῶν
φεύγοντας πεσέειν, δηΐοισι δὲ χάρμα γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
kai laon erykakete pro pylaōn
pantēi epoichomenoi prin aut’ en chersi gynaikōn
pheugontas peseein, dēïoisi de charma genesthai.
sentences.l:
and hold back the people before the gates,
going about everywhere, before again in the hands of women
they fall, fleeing, and become a joy to the enemy.
sentences.i: and hold the people back in front of the gates, going about everywhere, before they fall again, fleeing, into the arms of their women and become a joy to our enemies.
sentences.n: ἐρυκάκετε is a reduplicated aorist imperative of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’. πρὸ πυλάων is ‘in front of the gates’ (the epic genitive plural), and ἐποιχόμενοι is ‘going about among them’. πρὶν … πεσέειν is πρίν with an infinitive, ‘before they fall’ (πεσέειν = πεσεῖν), and αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again’. ἐν χερσὶ γυναικῶν ‘in the hands of women’ pictures the fleeing men tumbling into the arms of their wives. δηΐοισι ‘for the enemy’ goes with χάρμα, ‘a joy’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κε φάλαγγας ἐποτρύνητον ἁπάσας,
ἡμεῖς μὲν Δαναοῖσι μαχησόμεθ’ αὖθι μένοντες,
καὶ μάλα τειρόμενοί περ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei ke phalangas epotrynēton hapasas,
hēmeis men Danaoisi machēsometh’ authi menontes,
kai mala teiromenoi per·
sentences.i: but when you two have urged on all the battle-lines, we shall stay right here and fight the Danaans, though badly worn down;
sentences.n: ἐποτρύνητον is a dual subjunctive, ‘you two have urged on’ (Aeneas and Hector), with ἐπεί κε ‘when, once’ (= ἐπεὶ ἄν). ἡμεῖς μέν ‘we for our part’ is answered by Ἕκτορ ἀτάρ in line 86, ‘but you, Hector’. μαχησόμεθ’ is the future of μάχομαι, αὖθι is ‘right here’, and μένοντες is ‘staying, holding ground’. τειρόμενοι ‘worn down’ is the present passive participle of τείρω, and καὶ μάλα … περ is ‘even though greatly’.

sentences.t: ἀναγκαίη γὰρ ἐπείγει·
sentences.tr: anankaiē gar epeigei·
sentences.l: for compulsion presses hard;
sentences.i: for necessity presses us hard;
sentences.n: ἀναγκαίη is ἀνάγκη ‘necessity’ the longer epic form, the subject of ἐπείγει ‘presses’. γάρ ‘for’ says why they must stay and fight although they are worn down.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἀτὰρ σὺ πόλιν δὲ μετέρχεο, εἰπὲ δ’ ἔπειτα
μητέρι σῇ καὶ ἐμῇ·
sentences.tr:
Hektor atar sy polin de metercheo, eipe d’ epeita
mēteri sēi kai emēi·
sentences.l:
Hector, but you to the city go, and speak then
to your mother and mine;
sentences.i: But you, Hector, go on into the city, and then speak to your mother and mine:
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ turns from ‘we’ to Hector, and σύ underlines the contrast. πόλιν δέ is πόλιν with the suffix -δε of direction, ‘to the city’, and μετέρχεο is the imperative of μετέρχομαι ‘go on to’ (with uncontracted -εο). εἰπέ is the aorist imperative ‘speak’. μητέρι σῇ καὶ ἐμῇ is ‘to your mother and mine’: Helenus and Hector are brothers, as κασιγνήτῳ ‘brother’ in line 102 says. A message follows.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ ξυνάγουσα γεραιὰς
νηὸν Ἀθηναίης γλαυκώπιδος ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ
οἴξασα κληῗδι θύρας ἱεροῖο δόμοιο
πέπλον, ὅς οἱ δοκέει χαριέστατος ἠδὲ μέγιστος
εἶναι ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ καί οἱ πολὺ φίλτατος αὐτῇ,
sentences.tr:
hē de xynagousa geraias
nēon Athēnaiēs glaukōpidos en polei akrēi
oixasa klēïdi thyras hieroio domoio
peplon, hos hoi dokeei chariestatos ēde megistos
einai eni megarōi kai hoi poly philtatos autēi,
sentences.l:
and she, gathering the old women
to the temple of gleaming-eyed Athena in the high city,
having opened with the bolt the doors of the sacred house,
a robe, which seems to her most graceful and greatest
to be in the hall, and by far dearest to herself,
sentences.i: She is to gather the old women at the temple of gleaming-eyed Athena in the high city and, opening the doors of the sacred house with the bolt, take the robe that seems to her the most graceful and the greatest in the hall, and by far the dearest to her own self,
sentences.n: This is the start of the message, a single sentence that goes on to line 98. ἣ δέ is ‘and she’, the mother. ξυνάγουσα is συνάγουσα ‘gathering’ in the old spelling ξυν-, and γεραιάς is ‘old women’. νηόν ‘temple’ is an accusative of goal, and ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ is ‘in the high city’, on its summit. γλαυκώπιδος is ‘gleaming-eyed’, as in the house rendering of γλαυκῶπις. οἴξασα is the aorist participle of οἴγνυμι ‘open’, and κληῗδι is ‘with the bolt’ (the door’s fastening). ἱεροῖο δόμοιο is ‘of the sacred house’, with the epic genitive. In the Greek πέπλον ‘a robe’ waits for its verb, θεῖναι ‘to lay’, in the next unit; the English supplies ‘take’. ὅς οἱ δοκέει means ‘which seems to her’ (ὅς is the relative, οἱ ‘to her’), and χαριέστατος, μέγιστος and φίλτατος are superlatives: ‘most graceful’, ‘greatest’, ‘dearest’; αὐτῇ is ‘to her very self’.

sentences.t: θεῖναι Ἀθηναίης ἐπὶ γούνασιν ἠϋκόμοιο,
sentences.tr: theinai Athēnaiēs epi gounasin ēÿkomoio,
sentences.l: to lay on the knees of Athena, fine-haired,
sentences.i: and lay it on the knees of fine-haired Athena,
sentences.n: θεῖναι is the aorist infinitive of τίθημι ‘put, lay’, used for an order passed on (‘she is to lay’), and its object is the robe (πέπλον) of the last unit. The gift goes on the goddess’s knees, the place where a suppliant’s hands also go (compare line 45). γούνασιν is the epic dative plural of γόνυ ‘knee’, and ἠϋκόμοιο ‘fine-haired’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
καί οἱ ὑποσχέσθαι δυοκαίδεκα βοῦς ἐνὶ νηῷ
ἤνις ἠκέστας ἱερευσέμεν, αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ
ἄστύ τε καὶ Τρώων ἀλόχους καὶ νήπια τέκνα,
sentences.tr:
kai hoi hyposchesthai dyokaideka bous eni nēōi
ēnis ēkestas hiereusemen, ai k’ eleēsēi
asty te kai Trōōn alochous kai nēpia tekna,
sentences.l:
and to promise her twelve cows in the temple,
year-old, never-goaded, to sacrifice, if she will take pity on
the town and the Trojans’ wives and infant children,
sentences.i: and promise her twelve yearling heifers in the temple, never touched by the goad, to sacrifice, if she will take pity on the town and the wives of the Trojans and their little children,
sentences.n: ὑποσχέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ὑπισχνέομαι ‘promise’, a second order beside θεῖναι. ἐνὶ νηῷ is ἐν νηῷ ‘in the temple’ (νηός = Attic ναός), and ἱερευσέμεν is a future infinitive in -έμεν, ‘to sacrifice’, saying what is promised. ἤνις is ‘a year old’. The sense of ἠκέστας is not known with certainty; it is taken to mean ‘never goaded’, that is, not yet broken to the yoke. αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ is εἴ κε ἐλεήσῃ ‘if she will pity’, a hopeful condition with the subjunctive. ἄστυ ‘town’, ἀλόχους ‘wives’ and νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’ are all objects of ἐλεήσῃ.

sentences.t:
ὥς κεν Τυδέος υἱὸν ἀπόσχῃ Ἰλίου ἱρῆς
ἄγριον αἰχμητὴν κρατερὸν μήστωρα φόβοιο,
sentences.tr:
hōs ken Tydeos huion aposchēi Iliou hirēs
agrion aichmētēn krateron mēstōra phoboio,
sentences.l:
so that she may hold off from sacred Ilios the son of Tydeus,
the wild spearman, strong counsellor of flight,
sentences.i: so that she may keep the son of Tydeus away from sacred Ilios, that wild spearman, strong master of flight,
sentences.n: ὥς κεν … ἀπόσχῃ is a purpose clause, ‘so that she may hold (him) off’, with ἀπέχω taking the genitive Ἰλίου. Τυδέος υἱόν ‘the son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes, who has been killing in the first lines of this part. ἱρῆς is the Ionic form of ἱερῆς ‘sacred’. ἄγριον is ‘wild’, αἰχμητήν ‘spearman’, and κρατερόν ‘strong’. μήστωρα φόβοιο is ‘master of flight’: a μήστωρ is one who plans or commands, and φόβος in Homer is panic and flight. The same words are used at 5.272 of the pair of horses that Anchises gave to Aeneas.

sentences.t: ὃν δὴ ἐγὼ κάρτιστον Ἀχαιῶν φημι γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr: hon dē egō kartiston Achaiōn phēmi genesthai.
sentences.l: whom indeed I say to be the strongest of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: whom I declare to be the strongest of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ὃν δή is ‘whom indeed’. φημι with the infinitive γενέσθαι is ‘I say that he is’, and the aorist γενέσθαι ‘has turned out to be’ is close to εἶναι. κάρτιστος is the epic superlative of κρατερός ‘strong’ (Attic κράτιστος). This is why Helenus wants Diomedes held off.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ Ἀχιλῆά ποθ’ ὧδέ γ’ ἐδείδιμεν ὄρχαμον ἀνδρῶν,
ὅν πέρ φασι θεᾶς ἐξέμμεναι·
sentences.tr:
oud’ Achilēa poth’ hōde g’ edeidimen orchamon andrōn,
hon per phasi theas exemmenai·
sentences.l:
Not even Achilles ever so did we fear, chief of men,
whom indeed they say to be sprung from a goddess;
sentences.i: Never did we fear even Achilles, chief of men, like this, though they say he is born of a goddess;
sentences.n: Helenus now compares Diomedes with Achilles. οὐδ’ … ποτε ‘not even … ever’; Ἀχιλῆα has single λ, and ὄρχαμον ἀνδρῶν is ‘chief of men’. ἐδείδιμεν is ‘we feared’, a past tense of δείδω. ὅν πέρ is ‘him whom’, with πέρ giving the relative extra weight. ἐξέμμεναι is ἐξ and ἔμμεναι (= εἶναι), ‘to be sprung from’, with the genitive θεᾶς ‘a goddess’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅδε λίην
μαίνεται, οὐδέ τίς οἱ δύναται μένος ἰσοφαρίζειν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hode liēn
mainetai, oude tis hoi dynatai menos isopharizein.
sentences.l:
but this man exceedingly
rages, and no one is able to match him in might.”
sentences.i: but this man rages beyond all measure, and no one can match him in might.”
sentences.n: ὅδε ‘this one here’ is Diomedes, whom Helenus has just described. λίην is ‘exceedingly’, and μαίνεται ‘rages’ (from μαίνομαι) is the poem’s word for fighting frenzy. οἱ is ‘him’, the dative that ἰσοφαρίζειν ‘to match, to bear oneself as an equal’ takes after δύναται ‘is able’, and μένος is an accusative of respect, ‘in might’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, Ἕκτωρ δ’ οὔ τι κασιγνήτῳ ἀπίθησεν.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, Hektōr d’ ou ti kasignētōi apithēsen.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Hector in no way his brother disobeyed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector did not disobey his brother at all.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the speech-closing formula, ἔφαθ’ being ἔφατο ‘spoke’. κασιγνήτῳ ‘brother’ is Helenus. ἀπίθησεν is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’, which takes the dative, and οὔ τι is ‘in no way’. Hector acts at once in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε,
πάλλων δ’ ὀξέα δοῦρα κατὰ στρατὸν ᾤχετο πάντῃ
ὀτρύνων μαχέσασθαι, ἔγειρε δὲ φύλοπιν αἰνήν.
sentences.tr:
autika d’ ex ocheōn syn teuchesin alto chamaze,
pallōn d’ oxea doura kata straton ōicheto pantēi
otrynōn machesasthai, egeire de phylopin ainēn.
sentences.l:
and at once from the chariot, with his armour, he leapt to the ground,
and brandishing sharp spears he went through the army everywhere,
urging them to fight, and he roused fearsome battle-din.
sentences.i: and at once he leapt from his chariot to the ground in his armour, and brandishing sharp spears he went everywhere through the army, urging the men to fight, and he roused fearsome battle-din.
sentences.n: αὐτίκα δ’ marks how quickly Hector acts. ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘from the chariot’ (ὄχεα is a plural for one vehicle), σὺν τεύχεσιν ‘in his armour’, and ἆλτο ‘leapt’ is the aorist of ἅλλομαι, with χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ (-ζε of direction). πάλλων ‘brandishing’ goes with ὀξέα δοῦρα ‘sharp spears’; ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go’, and πάντῃ is ‘everywhere’. ὀτρύνων μαχέσασθαι is ‘urging them to fight’. ἔγειρε is a past tense of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’, and φύλοπιν αἰνήν is the ‘fearsome battle-din’ which line 1 said was left alone. These three lines are word for word 5.494–496.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἐλελίχθησαν καὶ ἐναντίοι ἔσταν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ elelichthēsan kai enantioi estan Achaiōn·
sentences.l: And they were whirled round and stood opposite the Achaeans;
sentences.i: They wheeled round and took their stand facing the Achaeans;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Trojans, who a moment ago were near to going back into Ilios (73–74). ἐλελίχθησαν is the aorist passive of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl round’, and ἔσταν is the epic ἔστησαν, ‘took their stand’. ἐναντίοι takes the genitive Ἀχαιῶν, ‘facing the Achaeans’. The line is the same as 5.497.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ὑπεχώρησαν, λῆξαν δὲ φόνοιο,
φὰν δέ τιν’ ἀθανάτων ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος
Τρωσὶν ἀλεξήσοντα κατελθέμεν, ὡς ἐλέλιχθεν.
sentences.tr:
Argeioi d’ hypechōrēsan, lēxan de phonoio,
phan de tin’ athanatōn ex ouranou asteroentos
Trōsin alexēsonta katelthemen, hōs elelichthen.
sentences.l:
and the Argives drew back, and ceased from slaughter,
and said that one of the immortals from starry heaven
to defend the Trojans had come down, as they had wheeled round.
sentences.i: The Argives gave ground and left off the slaughter, and said that some one of the immortals had come down from starry heaven to defend the Trojans, seeing how they had wheeled round.
sentences.n: Ἀργεῖοι is the army again, under its third name. ὑπεχώρησαν is ‘gave ground, withdrew’, and λῆξαν is the aorist of λήγω ‘cease’, with the genitive φόνοιο ‘from slaughter’. φάν is ἔφασαν ‘they said’ (φημί) without the augment. τιν’ ἀθανάτων is ‘some one of the immortals’, ἀλεξήσοντα is the future participle of ἀλέξω ‘defend’, ‘to be going to defend’, with the dative Τρωσίν, and κατελθέμεν is the aorist infinitive κατελθεῖν ‘to have come down’. ὡς ἐλέλιχθεν gives the reason: ἐλέλιχθεν is ἐλελίχθησαν, the verb of line 106, and the Trojans’ sudden turn is what makes the Argives think a god is with them.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δὲ Τρώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr: Hektōr de Trōessin ekekleto makron aÿsas·
sentences.l: And Hector to the Trojans called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Hector gave orders to the Trojans, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: This is the line used for Nestor at 66, with the speaker and the hearers changed. Τρώεσσιν is the epic dative plural in -εσσι(ν).

sentences.t:
Τρῶες ὑπέρθυμοι τηλεκλειτοί τ’ ἐπίκουροι
ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς,
sentences.tr:
Trōes hyperthymoi tēlekleitoi t’ epikouroi
aneres este philoi, mnēsasthe de thouridos alkēs,
sentences.l:
“Trojans high-spirited and far-famed allies,
men be, friends, and be mindful of impetuous might,
sentences.i: “Trojans, high-spirited, and you far-famed allies: be men, friends, and remember impetuous might,
sentences.n: Hector addresses two groups: the Trojans (ὑπέρθυμοι ‘high-spirited’) and the ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ (τηλεκλειτοί ‘far-famed’), the troops from outside Troy such as the Lycians of line 78. ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι is ‘be men, friends’ (ἀνέρες is the epic nominative plural of ἀνήρ), a call to show courage. μνήσασθε is the aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’, with the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγὼ βείω προτὶ Ἴλιον, ἠδὲ γέρουσιν
εἴπω βουλευτῇσι καὶ ἡμετέρῃς ἀλόχοισι
δαίμοσιν ἀρήσασθαι, ὑποσχέσθαι δ’ ἑκατόμβας.
sentences.tr:
ophr’ an egō beiō proti Ilion, ēde gerousin
eipō bouleutēisi kai hēmeterēis alochoisi
daimosin arēsasthai, hyposchesthai d’ hekatombas.
sentences.l:
until I go to Ilios, and to the elders
I tell, the counsellors, and to our wives,
to pray to the gods, and to promise hecatombs.”
sentences.i: until I have gone to Ilios and told the elders, the counsellors, and our wives to pray to the gods and to promise hecatombs.”
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ ἂν … βείω is ‘until I go’, with βείω the epic aorist subjunctive of βαίνω (Attic βῶ); προτί is πρός ‘to’. εἴπω with the dative and an infinitive is ‘tell (them) to’: the infinitives are ἀρήσασθαι ‘to pray’ and ὑποσχέσθαι ‘to promise’. γέρουσιν is the dative plural of γέρων ‘old man, elder’, βουλευτῇσι ‘counsellors’ is in apposition (epic -ῃσι), and ἡμετέρῃς ἀλόχοισι is ‘to our wives’, with ἡμετέρῃς the epic feminine dative plural. δαίμοσιν is ‘to the gods’, and ἑκατόμβας are ‘hecatombs’, great public sacrifices. Hector’s message to the city matches what Helenus asked for in lines 87–95. The speech ends here.
